subsystems.name: Feedstock extraction
subsystems.role: mines the raw material — silicates and metals — from asteroids, moons or Mercury rather than launching it from Earth.

subsystems.name: In-space refining and fabrication
subsystems.role: turns rock and metal into thin films and structures without an atmosphere or a gravity well to fight.

subsystems.name: Launch and transport
subsystems.role: moves fabricated material from a low-gravity body to its operating orbit at very low energy cost.

subsystems.name: Collector elements
subsystems.role: the swarm units themselves — thin reflectors or photovoltaic surfaces that intercept sunlight.

subsystems.name: Orbit and station keeping
subsystems.role: keeps millions of independent elements in stable, non-colliding heliocentric orbits — a swarm, not a solid shell.

subsystems.name: Power handling and transmission
subsystems.role: converts or relays the captured energy to where it is used.

subsystems.name: Autonomy and command
subsystems.role: runs a system too large and too slow to control from Earth in real time.

buildSteps.title: Survey and select feedstock
buildSteps.detail: Remote sensing and sample-return missions identify metal-rich near-Earth asteroids and the composition of Mercury's surface, and confirm which materials can be refined cheaply in vacuum.

buildSteps.title: Land and mine at low gravity
buildSteps.detail: Robotic excavators anchor themselves, break up regolith and ore, and bag or crush material for processing. Low gravity makes this physically easy but mechanically awkward — anchoring and dust are the hard parts.

buildSteps.title: Refine in space
buildSteps.detail: Concentrated sunlight smelts metal; vacuum and microgravity allow extremely thin films and large trusses that would sag or oxidise on Earth.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the collector units
buildSteps.detail: Rolling mills and deposition lines produce kilometres-wide, micron-thin reflectors or solar cells, plus the minimum frame and control hardware needed to keep them oriented.

buildSteps.title: Launch without rockets
buildSteps.detail: An electromagnetic launcher on an airless, low-escape-velocity body throws packaged material onto transfer orbits. Mercury's escape velocity of about 4.3 km/s is far lower than Earth's 11.2 km/s, and there is no atmosphere to push through.

buildSteps.title: Deploy into heliocentric orbit
buildSteps.detail: Tugs or sails spiral each unit out to its assigned orbit, likely near the Sun where sunlight is strongest and the same collector area intercepts far more power.

buildSteps.title: Bootstrap self-replication
buildSteps.detail: A seed factory builds copies of itself from local material, so the number of units grows exponentially rather than linearly — the step that makes a swarm possible at all.

buildSteps.title: Operate the swarm
buildSteps.detail: Units either convert sunlight to beamed power, or act as a computational substrate. Earth or an orbital habitat receives the energy.

buildSteps.title: Maintain and expand
buildSteps.detail: Debris, micrometeorites and orbital drift are managed continuously, and coverage of the Sun's output grows over centuries as more material is processed.

prerequisites.why: a swarm needs more mass than any launch programme could ever lift; only exponential in-space industry makes it feasible.

prerequisites.tech: Off-Earth mining and refining at industrial scale
prerequisites.why: without local material, every kilogram of collector must be lifted out of Earth's gravity well.
mass drivers, solar sails and electric propulsion have all flown, but not at the throughput or reliability required.

prerequisites.tech: Wireless power transmission at high power
prerequisites.why: beaming energy over long distances has been demonstrated only at small scale in experiments.
millions of independent orbiting elements must avoid each other and stay on station without ground control.
modelling shows swarms can be stable where a solid shell is not, but the engineering is unproven.

pathway.milestone: robotic asteroid sample return and small in-space assembly experiments
pathway.unlocks: knowledge of what off-Earth material is actually like to handle.

pathway.milestone: first self-sustaining orbital refineries and large solar power satellites
pathway.unlocks: industry that grows without resupply from Earth.

pathway.milestone: self-replicating factories producing collector units from asteroid metal
pathway.unlocks: exponential growth in installed collector area.

pathway.milestone: a growing swarm that intercepts a measurable fraction of the Sun's ~3.8 × 10^26 W output
pathway.unlocks: a waste-heat infrared signature detectable across interstellar distances — the classic Dyson signature described by Freeman Dyson in 1960.

pathway.milestone: full capture of solar output — roughly 10^26 W, the Kardashev Type II threshold
pathway.unlocks: energy and computation resources many orders of magnitude beyond Earth's current use.
